title: The Return of the Night Train
text: Across Europe, sleeper trains that were written off as relics two decades ago are being rebuilt, and the arguments used to bury them are now being used to revive them. Operators once claimed that no traveller would trade a ninety-minute flight for eleven hours in a bunk. What they underestimated was how much of a short-haul journey is spent not flying: the airport transfer, the queue, the wait. If those hours were counted honestly, the night train would already have looked competitive. Critics respond, fairly, that sleeper carriages are expensive to run, since a bed sells once while an aircraft seat may sell four times a day. Subsidy, then, is unavoidable, and the honest question is not whether the state should pay but what it is paying for. A government that taxes aviation fuel while starving the railway is not neutral; it has simply chosen a slower kind of subsidy. Night trains may never carry the majority of travellers. They tend, however, to change what the majority considers normal, and that shift is worth buying.

author: Elena Marchetti

title: Forty Dutch Words
text: A study carried out at a university in Freiburg tested a claim that language teachers have repeated for years: that new vocabulary is consolidated during sleep. Sixty adult learners were taught forty Dutch words in the evening. Half were allowed to sleep for eight hours; the others stayed awake and were tested at the same clock time the following morning, so that fatigue was distributed evenly across both groups. The sleepers recalled roughly twenty per cent more items. What the researchers regard as the more interesting result, however, concerns which words survived. Items that had been linked to an existing German cognate were retained almost equally by both groups, while isolated, unfamiliar forms benefited most from sleep. This suggests that sleep may not strengthen memory in general so much as rescue material that has nothing else to hold on to. The authors are cautious. A single laboratory night with young, motivated volunteers tells us little about a teenager revising for an examination after four nights of five hours.

By teaching both groups their word list in the morning instead
By testing both groups at the same clock time the following morning

By removing every word that resembled a German cognate

qs.evidence: were tested at the same clock time the following morning
qs.answer: By testing both groups at the same clock time the following morning

qs.evidence: while isolated, unfamiliar forms benefited most from sleep
qs.answer: Cognates survived almost equally in both groups, while isolated forms gained most from sleep

qs.evidence: rescue material that has nothing else to hold on to
qs.answer: Sleep may act less as a general strengthener than as a rescue for unsupported material

qs.answer: To show how far the laboratory condition sits from real revision

author: Ingrid Halvorsen

title: Week Three on the Mudflat
text: Notes from the eastern edge of the delta, week three. The plantation we were shown last year has thinned badly. Of the seedlings pushed into the mud in 2019, perhaps one in five is still standing, and the survivors are clustered where a creek keeps the sediment soft. Villagers had warned the contractors about the site. Mangroves are not a single crop; each species tolerates a narrow band of salt and tide, and the fast-growing variety chosen for the photographs was planted well above the line where it can breathe. Had the planners walked the mudflat at low tide with the fishers, the failure would have been obvious before a single seedling was ordered. What is striking is that the restoration is still recorded as complete. Hectares planted, not hectares surviving, is the figure the funding cycle rewards. Two kilometres north, where no money was spent and grazing was simply banned, the forest has closed over on its own. That contrast is uncomfortable, and it is the one the final report will probably omit.

Because the species chosen was planted above the tidal line it can tolerate

qs.evidence: was planted well above the line where it can breathe
qs.answer: Because the species chosen was planted above the tidal line it can tolerate

author: Prosenjit Barua

title: A Wage Floor, Discussed
text:
Q: For decades the textbooks said that a higher minimum wage destroys jobs. Has that changed?
A: The textbook prediction assumed an employer who can hire as many workers as she likes at the going rate. In many towns there are only two or three large employers, and they set the rate rather than accept it. Under those conditions a modest rise can increase employment, because more people are willing to take the job at all.
Q: The word modest is doing a great deal of work in that sentence.
A: It is, deliberately. Nobody serious claims the effect holds at any level. If the floor were raised to twice the median wage tomorrow, I would expect closures, and anyone who told you otherwise would be selling something.
Q: Then why is the debate still so bitter?
A: Partly because both sides quote studies from different labour markets as though they described the same country. And partly because the losses, when they come, fall on people who never appear in the average. A restaurant that never opens employs nobody, and nobody counts it.

qs.evidence: a modest rise can increase employment
qs.answer: Where only a few employers dominate, a moderate rise can raise employment

author: Tomas Ruiz

title: Nostalgia as an Instrument
text: Every studio executive now knows that the safest film to finance is one the audience has already seen. Remakes and sequels reduce the terrifying question of whether anyone wants this to the manageable question of whether anyone remembers it. The result is not, as the angrier critics insist, a collapse in imagination. Craft is often superb; the money is on the screen. What has narrowed is the range of things a mainstream film is permitted to be about. A story that arrives with no prior audience must earn attention from nothing, and attention has become the scarcest input in the industry. If risk were spread across a whole slate, as it once was, a studio could absorb four failures for one surprise. Streaming has made that arithmetic harder to defend to shareholders who can watch cancellation figures by the hour. Nostalgia, then, is less a taste than a financing instrument. Audiences are blamed for wanting the familiar, yet they are rarely offered a comparable budget attached to anything else, and preference measured under those conditions tells us very little.

qs.answer: Nostalgia in cinema is driven mainly by financing logic rather than by public taste

qs.evidence: Craft is often superb; the money is on the screen.
qs.answer: the budget is visibly reflected in the production quality

author: Dalia Ferreira

title: Inside the Sandstone Mountain
text: Cut into a sandstone mountain on a Norwegian island, the Svalbard Global Seed Vault is often described as a doomsday store, a phrase its staff quietly dislike. The vault holds duplicates. Each box remains the property of the gene bank that deposited it, and only that depositor may withdraw it, which makes the building less an ark than a safety deposit facility for agriculture. Its first withdrawal, in 2015, followed not a meteor or a plague but a civil war that cut researchers off from their collection in Aleppo. Those seeds were multiplied in Lebanon and Morocco and then redeposited, which is exactly how the system is meant to work. Permafrost was expected to keep the chambers cold without power. Warming has already forced the installation of mechanical cooling and a waterproofed entrance tunnel, an irony noted by every journalist who visits. The vault protects against a narrow set of risks. Whether crop diversity survives depends far more on the underfunded national gene banks whose losses it can only mirror, never prevent.
qs: Apa fungsi utama brankas benih ini menurut teks?
To store duplicate collections that only the depositor may withdraw
To gather every seed variety on earth for open public use
To breed new crop varieties suited to the Norwegian climate
To replace national gene banks that are running out of money

qs.evidence: only that depositor may withdraw it
qs.answer: To store duplicate collections that only the depositor may withdraw

qs.answer: war cut off the Aleppo collection, seeds were withdrawn, multiplied abroad, then redeposited

author: Karin Lund

title: Two Ways to Open a Book
text: Two philosophies have fought over the teaching of reading for half a century. The first treats decoding as the core task: children are taught the relationship between letters and sounds systematically, in a fixed order, before meaning is emphasised. The second treats reading as the pursuit of meaning, with children guessing unfamiliar words from pictures and context, on the assumption that decoding will follow naturally, as speech does. Large reviews now favour the first approach for beginners, particularly for children who arrive at school with small vocabularies and nobody at home to read with them. That finding is often reported as a total victory, which it is not. Systematic phonics reliably gets children off the page and into words; it does not by itself produce readers who understand what they have decoded. Comprehension depends on background knowledge that no phonics programme supplies. The strongest classrooms borrow from both traditions, and the fiercest advocates on either side tend to be arguing about a stage of learning rather than about reading as a whole.

qs.evidence: children are taught the relationship between letters and sounds systematically
qs.answer: one teaches letter and sound relations systematically, the other treats guessing meaning as primary

qs: Kelompok anak mana yang paling diuntungkan oleh pendekatan pertama?

qs.evidence: children who arrive at school with small vocabularies
qs.answer: Children with small vocabularies and nobody at home to read with them

author: Grace Achebe

title: Pricing the Road in Stockholm
text: Policy note: pricing the road. When Stockholm introduced a charge for driving into the city centre in 2006, it did so as a trial, with a referendum promised at the end. Support before the trial stood at around a third of residents. Seven months later, after traffic had fallen by roughly a fifth and journey times had become predictable, a narrow majority voted to keep it. The sequence matters more than the numbers. Had the referendum been held first, the scheme would almost certainly have been rejected, and it is difficult to imagine the trial being authorised afterwards. Opponents had argued that shops in the centre would empty; retail turnover did not fall. They had also argued that the charge was regressive, and here the objection carries more force, since a flat fee weighs more heavily on a low income. The city answered by spending the revenue on public transport, which is a compensation rather than a correction. Cities copying the design should note that what made it survivable was not the economics but the order in which citizens were asked.

a trial first, then a referendum seven months later

qs.evidence: it did so as a trial, with a referendum promised at the end
qs.answer: a trial first, then a referendum seven months later

author: Anders Sjoberg

title: Thinking With Eight Arms
text: An octopus has about five hundred million neurons, comparable to a dog, but two thirds of them sit in its arms rather than its brain. Each arm can taste what it touches and can solve a small problem, such as working a limb into a crevice, while the animal attends to something else entirely. Researchers who describe this as distributed intelligence are careful to add that we do not know what, if anything, it is like to be such a creature. Experiments have shown that octopuses recognise individual keepers, learn to open jars, and, in captivity, appear to grow bored. A famous account of one animal squirting water at a light bulb it disliked circulates so widely that its evidential status is rarely questioned. This is the difficulty. The behaviour is genuinely strange, so anecdote and data are easily confused, and a field that depends on charming stories risks losing the scepticism that would make its claims stick. If octopus cognition were less appealing, it might be studied more rigorously.

qs.answer: Mostly in its arms rather than its brain

author: Miriam Kessler

title: The Wrong Argument for Coding
text: The proposal to make programming compulsory for every secondary pupil is usually defended on economic grounds: the jobs are there, and the country needs them filled. That argument is weaker than it looks. Labour forecasts have a poor record, and a curriculum designed around the shortages of one decade may equip a generation for a market that has moved on by the time they graduate. A better defence exists, and supporters rarely make it. Writing a program forces a pupil to state a procedure so precisely that a machine can follow it, and to accept that a failure belongs to the instructions rather than to the listener. Very little else in school teaches that discipline so unforgivingly. If coding were taught as a way of thinking rather than as vocational training, the shallow criticism that not everyone will become a developer would lose its force, since not everyone who studies geometry becomes a surveyor. The risk is that ministers, who must justify budgets within a single term, will keep choosing the argument that sounds urgent over the one that lasts.

to replace the economic case for coding with a stronger educational one
to compare several programming languages used in schools

author: Owen Trask

title: The Price of a Light Metal
text: Between 2021 and 2023 the price of lithium carbonate rose roughly sixfold and then gave most of it back. Commentators reached for the language of scarcity, yet lithium is not rare, and known reserves would cover projected demand for decades. What is scarce is processing capacity and the permission to build it. A new mine takes between seven and fifteen years to move from discovery to first shipment, most of that time spent waiting for permits, while a battery factory can be finished in two. When demand accelerates, the two clocks fall out of step, and the price does the adjusting. Producers respond by opening capacity, which arrives late and all at once, and the crash that follows discourages the next round of investment. If the cycle is understood as a mismatch of lead times rather than a shortage of rock, the policy conclusion changes: subsidising extraction may do less than shortening the approval process. Neither option is politically comfortable, which is one reason the cycle tends to repeat itself.
qs: Bagaimana penulis menjelaskan lonjakan harga litium?
By pointing to a genuine global shortage of the metal in the earth
By blaming speculation in commodity markets and nothing else
By contrasting the time needed to open a mine with the time needed to build a factory

author: Priya Nandakumar

title: When the Clocks Agreed
text: Before the railways, every town kept its own noon, set by the sun overhead, and nobody found this inconvenient. A traveller who arrived in a city half an hour behind his own watch simply adjusted it. What made local time intolerable was the timetable. Trains running on lines that crossed a dozen local noons produced collisions and missed connections, and the companies, not governments, imposed the first uniform standard, printing their own time on station clocks and daring the towns to disagree. Some resisted for years, and a few clock faces in England carried two minute hands. The lesson usually drawn is that technology forced a rational reform on a superstitious public. That reading flatters us. Local time had been perfectly rational for the purposes it served, and the new standard was not more accurate, only more shared. What the railways changed was not the sun but the cost of disagreement. Similar arguments now surround file formats, plugs and measurement systems, where the winning standard is seldom the best one, merely the one that arrived when coordination had become expensive enough to buy.

author: Hugh Cormack

title: Where the Shade Went
text: A survey of one southwestern American city found that the difference in summer afternoon temperature between its wealthiest and poorest districts reached almost seven degrees. The cause is not mysterious. Tree canopy covers roughly a quarter of the ground in the older, richer neighbourhoods and less than five per cent in the districts built after 1960, where wide roads and parking lots absorb sunlight all day and release it after dark. Planting programmes have been announced repeatedly. Their weakness is that a tree is not a light bulb: it must be watered for years before it shades anything, and the households expected to water it are frequently tenants who may not be living there when the shade arrives. Where the city has paid a small monthly sum to residents who agree to maintain a street tree, survival rates after three years have roughly doubled. That is a modest, unglamorous intervention, and it is far cheaper than the cooling centres opened each July. Whether it can be scaled before the next decade of heat is a separate question, and nobody in the department sounds confident.

author: Rosa Delgado

title: Money With No Conditions
text: Two experiments are usually cited in arguments about unconditional cash. In a two-year Finnish trial, unemployed people who received a monthly payment with no obligations were slightly more likely to be in work at the end than the control group, though the difference was small; what changed clearly was reported stress and trust in institutions. In a long-running Kenyan programme, villages received transfers large enough to matter, and researchers recorded new businesses, more schooling and no measurable rise in spending on alcohol, a fear that had dominated the debate beforehand. Reading the two together is tempting and slightly dishonest. The Finnish payment replaced an existing benefit within a wealthy welfare state; the Kenyan transfer arrived where almost nothing else did. A policy that mainly buys dignity in Helsinki may buy capital in a village, and evidence for one claim is routinely presented as evidence for the other. Supporters would strengthen their case by saying which of the two effects they are promising, since a scheme sold as a growth policy will be judged, eventually, by growth.

author: Lars Ekstrom

title: The Station Above the Bakery
text: The transmitter sits in a room above a bakery, and the aerial is guyed to a water tank. Radio Ayni broadcasts for nine hours a day in Aymara and Spanish, and its most popular programme is not the news but a slot in which listeners telephone messages to relatives who have no telephone. Somebody in the valley will hear it and walk the message up the hill. Founded by a miners union in the 1970s, the station survived two periods in which it was closed and its equipment removed. Younger volunteers now argue that its future lies online, and they are half right: the archive of recordings has found an audience among migrants in Buenos Aires. Yet the households the station was built for often have electricity for only part of the day, and a battery radio asks nothing of them. If the schedule were moved to a platform requiring data, the audience that gives the station its purpose would be the first to disappear. The volunteers know this. They are arguing, really, about who the station is for.

author: Claudia Mamani

title: Pills That Announce Themselves
text: For a century the placebo effect was assumed to require deception. A trial at a Boston hospital tested whether it does. Patients with long-standing digestive pain were given a bottle labelled, in plain language, as containing inert pills, and were told directly that the tablets contained no active medicine. They were also told, truthfully, that placebos have produced measurable improvement in many studies and that the body can respond to a treatment ritual. Reported symptoms fell more in this group than in a group offered no treatment at all. The result has since been repeated for back pain and for fatigue, though the effect sizes are modest and the outcomes are all self-reported, which matters, because pain is precisely the sort of thing that improves when a patient believes somebody is paying attention. What the study appears to challenge is not the existence of the placebo effect but the story told about it. If honesty does not destroy the response, then belief in a specific chemical may matter less than the shape of the encounter itself.

author: Nadia Farouk

title: Fractions of a Cent
text: A song streamed a million times may earn its writer less than a single well-attended concert. This is usually blamed on the platforms, and their share is indeed large, but the arithmetic that hurts most working musicians happens earlier. Revenue is pooled: every subscription in a country is added together, and the pot is divided according to each track's share of total plays. A listener who plays one obscure album on repeat all month therefore funds the artists at the top of the chart, not the album he actually listened to. Under a user-centric model, his subscription would follow his own listening instead. Trials suggest such a change would move only a few per cent of the money, which sounds trivial until one notices where those percentages land: on artists with small, devoted audiences, precisely the group least able to absorb a bad year. Labels resist the change, partly because the accounting is harder and partly because they benefit from the present distribution. The argument is often framed as technical. It is a question about who counts as a listener.

author: Bea Okonjo

title: Amphorae at Thirty Metres
text: The wreck lies at thirty metres, shallow enough for divers and deep enough that trawlers have left it largely intact. We recorded the site over eleven days before lifting anything. The cargo is mixed: amphorae from at least three production centres, a crate of unfinished bronze fittings, and a small quantity of raw glass, still in the lumps in which it was traded. Mixed cargoes complicate the tidy picture of ancient trade running between fixed pairs of ports. A ship carrying goods from three regions was probably calling at several harbours, buying and selling as prices allowed, which is closer to peddling than to shipping. Dating rests on the amphorae, since the glass could have travelled for decades before being loaded. One team member argued for lifting the bronze immediately; the conservation laboratory was full, and an object raised without a place to go often deteriorates faster than one left in the sediment. It stayed down. Publication will take four years, which visitors find astonishing and archaeologists consider brisk.

author: Selin Aydin

title: The Glue in the Case
text: A washing machine that fails after seven years is not a scandal in itself. What deserves scrutiny is why the failure is so often terminal. Control boards are paired to serial numbers, fasteners are replaced by adhesive, and diagnostic codes are withheld from anyone outside an authorised network, so a repair that would take an hour becomes a purchase instead. Manufacturers defend these choices on grounds of safety and reliability, and the defence is not empty: a sealed unit really can be more waterproof. It is also, conveniently, more profitable. Recent legislation in several countries now requires spare parts to be available for a decade and manuals to be published, which is progress, though a right to buy a part is worth little if the part costs two thirds of a new machine. The deeper problem is that repair competes with a business model rather than with a technical limit. Until the price of a spare board is regulated, or the cost of replacement is charged to whoever designs the glue, the law will keep addressing the symptom.

author: Martin Kelleher

title: Rails or Rubber
text: Cities choosing between bus rapid transit and light rail are usually presented with a cost comparison, and on that measure the bus wins comfortably: a dedicated busway can be built for a fraction of the price per kilometre and opened years earlier. The comparison is fair as far as it goes. What it omits is that the two systems make different promises to a landowner. Rails are difficult to remove, so a developer who builds beside a tram line is buying a commitment; a bus lane can be repainted as a general traffic lane by a future council in a weekend. This is why light rail is more often followed by dense construction along its corridor, an effect that is sometimes reported as though the vehicles themselves attracted investment. In cities where the busway has been given legal protection and its stations built in concrete, buses have produced similar development. The choice, then, is less about rubber and steel than about how credibly a city can bind its own hands.
